item.title: Kobe Beef: The World's Most Famous Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Kobe beef is the most famous wagyu on earth, and unusually for a global brand it is tightly defined: only carcasses from purebred Tajima cattle, born, raised and slaughtered in Hyogo Prefecture and meeting strict marbling and weight grades, may carry the name — a few thousand animals a year. The Tajima breed from northern Hyogo is the source of that quality, its meat threaded with exceptionally fine marbling that melts at low temperature.

item.title: Kumano Beef: Wakayama's Mountain-Raised Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Kumano beef (Kumano-gyu) is Wakayama’s premium wagyu brand, raised in small numbers in the mountains of the Kii Peninsula where clean air, pure water and careful feeding produce beef with fine marbling and a notably sweet fat. Because production is small compared with the famous national brands, it is mostly eaten within the region, making it something of a local secret — served as grilled steak, yakiniku, shabu-shabu or in donburi at restaurants around Tanabe, Shingu and the Kumano area.

item.title: Matsusaka Beef Festival: Prize Wagyu and Affordable Feasts — Guide
item.description: The Matsusaka Beef Festival (Matsusaka Ushi Matsuri), held each November in the wagyu’s home town, is the year’s great celebration of Japan’s most luxurious beef. Its centrepiece is a prestigious cattle-judging competition in which the finest Matsusaka cows are paraded and ranked, the champion fetching astonishing prices — but for visitors the real draw is the chance to eat: festival stalls and special sales offer premium Matsusaka beef, from grilled skewers to bento and cuts to take home, at prices far below the usual, in a rare democratic feast of one of the world’s most exclusive foods.

item.title: Matsusaka Beef: Japan's Most Luxurious Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Matsusaka beef is among the most prestigious and expensive wagyu in Japan, ranked with Kobe and Omi at the very top of the country’s beef. It comes from virgin female cattle raised with legendary care in and around the castle town of Matsusaka — famously massaged and, in old lore, given beer to stimulate appetite — over an unusually long fattening period that produces an extraordinarily fine, low-melting marble that dissolves on the tongue.

item.title: Omi Beef: Japan's Oldest Wagyu Brand — Guide
item.description: Omi beef is Japan’s oldest wagyu brand, raised in Shiga’s mild lake basin for over 400 years and famously supplied to the Tokugawa shoguns as ‘medicinal’ miso-cured beef in an age when eating meat was officially taboo. Counted with Kobe and Matsusaka among Japan’s top three wagyu, it is prized for silken, fine-grained marbling with a low melting point that dissolves on the tongue, and Shiga serves it every way: bubbling sukiyaki in century-old restaurants, charcoal-grilled steak, shabu-shabu, and affordable lunchtime beef bowls in the castle towns of Hikone and Omihachiman.

item.title: Hida Beef: Gifu's Premium Marbled Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Hida beef is one of Japan’s top premium wagyu brands, produced from black-haired cattle raised in the Hida region of Gifu and prized for its fine, delicate marbling, melt-in-the-mouth tenderness and rich, sweet flavour. It is served across Takayama and the wider region in many forms, from steak and hoba-miso (grilled over a magnolia leaf with miso) to Hida beef sushi, croquettes and grilled skewers sold as street food in the old town, giving visitors plenty of ways to sample it at every price point.

item.title: Hitachi Beef: Ibaraki's Premium Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Hitachi beef (Hitachi-gyu) is Ibaraki’s premium wagyu brand, raised on the prefecture’s rich pastureland under strict quality standards that govern feed, breeding and grading. Known for its fine, even marbling and tender texture, the beef is served across the prefecture in dedicated steakhouses, yakiniku grill restaurants and traditional sukiyaki and shabu-shabu establishments, offering a genuine taste of high-grade Japanese wagyu outside the more famous Kobe or Matsusaka brands. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Various towns across Ibaraki Hours Lunch & dinner, restaurant-dependent Admission Set meals typically ¥3,000–8,000+ Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Maesawa Beef: Iwate's Top-Brand Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Maesawa beef, raised in Oshu in southern Iwate, is one of Japan’s top wagyu brands — prized for its fine marbling and melt-in-the-mouth tenderness. Savoured as steak, sukiyaki, shabu-shabu or even nigiri sushi, it rivals the famous beef of Kobe and Matsusaka at friendlier prices in its home region. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Oshu & Morioka, Iwate Hours Restaurant hours Admission Premium; varies by cut Time needed About 1.

item.title: Yamagata Beef: Clean, Sweet Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Yamagata beef (Yamagata Gyu) is one of Japan’s certified branded wagyu strains — raised on the clean mountain water and feed of the Shonai and Okitama regions, the cattle develop exceptional marbling and a distinctively clean, sweet fat that distinguishes it from Kobe or Matsusaka styles. Look for it as shabu-shabu, sukiyaki or grilled thinly over charcoal at specialist restaurants in Yamagata City. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yamagata City & beyond Hours Restaurant hours Admission Premium; varies by cut Time needed About 1.

item.title: Yonezawa Beef: One of Japan's Three Great Wagyu — Guide
item.description: Yonezawa beef is one of Japan’s three great wagyu brands alongside Matsusaka and Kobe, prized for its extraordinary fat marbling, buttery texture and delicate sweetness. Cattle raised in the Okitama basin are fed on local rice straw and pure mountain water, producing meat so tender it dissolves on the tongue. Specialty yakiniku and sukiyaki houses in Yonezawa City serve the full spectrum of cuts. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Yonezawa, Yamagata Hours Restaurant hours Admission Premium; varies by cut Time needed About 1.

item.title: Tottori Food Guide: Matsuba Crab, 20th Century Pears & Wagyu Beef
item.description: Tottori’s food identity is built on cold-water ingredients and patient agriculture. The Sea of Japan delivers premium snow crab and hatahata fish; the mild coastal climate and good soil produce pears that dominate national supply; and local ranchers in the Daisen foothills raise wagyu that rivals more famous brands at lower prices. This is a prefecture where eating well requires knowing the season and going to the right source. Matsuba Crab (Snow Crab) Tottori leads western Japan in snow crab catch, and the local brand — Matsuba Kani — commands serious respect among Japanese food enthusiasts.

item.title: Gunma Food Guide: Mizusawa Udon, Wagyu & Local Cuisine
item.description: Gunma is not a prefecture that features prominently on most food tourism itineraries, but that is largely because visitors tend to pass through rather than stop. Those who do stop find a food culture built around mountain vegetables, hot spring eggs, premium beef, and one of Japan’s most revered noodle traditions. The ingredients are honest and locally sourced, the settings are often intimate, and the price-to-quality ratio consistently surprises. Mizusawa Udon — One of Japan’s Top Three Mizusawa udon is listed alongside Sanuki udon from Kagawa and Inaniwa udon from Akita as one of the three great udon traditions of Japan.

item.title: Ibaraki Food Guide: Natto, Monkfish Hot Pot & Hitachi Beef
item.description: Ibaraki does not feature prominently on most food-travel itineraries, which makes it all the more interesting for travellers who eat seriously. The prefecture borders the Pacific, sits on some of Japan’s most productive agricultural land, and has a coastline that draws cold, nutrient-rich currents — conditions that produce exceptional ingredients across every category. Mito is the fermented soybean capital of Japan. The port town of Oarai supplies winter monkfish so prized that Japanese chefs use the word “winter in Ibaraki” as shorthand for the dish.

item.title: Mie Food Guide: Matsusaka Beef, Ise Lobster & Pearl Bay Seafood
item.description: Mie is one of Japan’s most rewarding food destinations. It lies at the intersection of two food cultures that rarely overlap: a premium beef tradition of the highest calibre, centred on the inland city of Matsusaka, and a Pacific coastal seafood tradition that draws on the exceptionally clean waters of Ago Bay and the Kumano Coast. The two rarely appear on the same table, and that is part of the pleasure of visiting — each meal in Mie feels like an argument for an entirely different region of Japan.

item.title: Okayama Food Guide: Barazushi, White Peaches, and Mamakari
item.description: Okayama Prefecture calls itself Harenokuni — Land of Sunshine — and the name is directly relevant to its food culture. With Japan’s lowest rainfall and more annual sunshine hours than almost any other prefecture, Okayama’s agriculture produces some of the country’s finest fruit, while the Seto Inland Sea at its southern coast supplies exceptional seafood. The local food traditions that have grown from these resources are varied, locally distinct, and worth seeking out beyond the standard tourist lunch.

item.title: Shiga Food Guide: Omi Beef, Funazushi, and Lake Biwa Cuisine
item.description: Shiga Prefecture’s food identity is shaped almost entirely by Lake Biwa. The lake provides a suite of endemic freshwater fish that appear nowhere else on Japanese menus, and the pastures and rice paddies of the surrounding basin have nurtured Japan’s oldest named wagyu beef tradition. Eating well in Shiga means understanding these local ingredients — and being willing to venture beyond the expected. Omi Beef — Japan’s Oldest Wagyu Brand Most visitors know Kobe beef.

item.title: Best Wagyu Beef in Japan Where to Eat Guide
item.description: Best Wagyu Beef in Japan: Where to Eat Guide for the Ultimate Beef Experience There is no food experience on Earth quite like eating authentic wagyu beef in Japan. If you’ve come across this best wagyu beef in Japan where to eat guide, you’re already on the right track — but let me be honest with you: after fifteen years of living here, exploring every corner of this country, and eating more wagyu than my doctor would probably approve of, I can tell you that what most tourists experience as “wagyu” barely scratches the surface.
